The demo's `abstention_correct` is {{v1.mean_abstention_correct|.1f}} for v1 and {{v2.mean_abstention_correct|.1f}} for v2 and v3: of the {{v2.n_abstention_correct}} unanswerable questions, v1 refuses {{v1.n_abstained|count}} and v2 {{v2.n_abstained|count}}. The measurement behind that failure is in the README: with idf weighting, unanswerable queries produce top retrieval scores between {{abl.abstention_separability.idf.unanswerable_top_min|.4f}} and {{abl.abstention_separability.idf.unanswerable_top_max|.4f}}, while {{abl.abstention_separability.idf.answerable_at_or_below_max}} of the {{abl.abstention_separability.idf.n_answerable}} answerable queries score no higher than that, so any `min_score` that rejects every unanswerable query also rejects most answerable ones; fixing it requires semantic matching, not threshold tuning. The point is what the evaluator did: it converted a vague worry ("does the system hallucinate on out-of-domain questions?") into a measured capability gap with the score distributions to prove it, and the regression reports carried that gap across versions instead of burying it under averages that looked acceptable. The metric rests on {{v2.n_abstention_correct}} cases, which is enough to show the gap but not to measure a small improvement; `abstention_accuracy` and `false_refusal` cover the answerable side.
